content: HIV can significantly impact lung development in children and adolescents, not only limiting their full lung potential but also increasing the risk of chronic lung disease in adulthood. A study conducted in South Africa observed a decline in lung function over two years among adolescents aged 9–16 years living with HIV, despite being on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Diagnostic tools for chronic lung disease, such as spirometry and high-resolution computed tomography, are often unavailable in low-income settings. Consequently, chronic respiratory symptoms are frequently treated empirically with repeated antibiotics and anti-tuberculosis (TB) therapy in regions with high HIV and TB prevalence. There are currently no specific guidelines for managing chronic lung disease associated with HIV. However, preventing lung infections through routine vaccinations (e.g., pneumococcal conjugate and annual influenza vaccines), early ART initiation, continued co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, isoniazid preventive therapy, avoiding tobacco smoke and indoor air pollution, and optimizing nutrition can help reduce the burden of chronic lung disease and improve lung health in children living with HIV. Neurodevelopmental delays, neurocognitive disorders, and mental health challenges are common among children living with HIV, particularly those who begin ART after infancy. A study of children aged 5–11 years from four sub-Saharan African countries found that children living with HIV performed worse in all cognitive domains compared to children who were either HIV-exposed but uninfected or not exposed to HIV. Despite effective ART, neurocognitive impairments may result from multiple factors, including ongoing viral replication in the central nervous system (CNS), neuroinflammation, irreversible CNS injury before ART initiation, ART-related neurotoxicity, and socioeconomic or psychosocial stressors. These impairments are often subtle and may go undetected during routine testing. Screening tools and culturally validated definitions for neurocognitive disorders are limited. A 2019 South African study validated an international HIV dementia screening tool for young people. Mental health disorders, such as depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and behavioral issues, are highly prevalent among children and adolescents living with HIV, with adolescents being more affected than younger children. These disorders often coexist and are associated with poor functional competence, self-concept, and motivation, as well as higher levels of depression, disruptive behavior, and clinically significant anger compared to HIV-negative peers. Psychosocial stressors, including stigma, discrimination, parental illness or death, and unstable guardianship, further exacerbate mental health vulnerabilities in children living with HIV. Mental health disorders can negatively impact ART adherence and quality of life but often receive less attention than physical health concerns. Since many adult mental health issues originate in childhood or adolescence, early screening and intervention are critical. Children living with HIV who experience advanced immunosuppression before starting ART or initiate ART at an older age face a higher risk of developing cancers, such as Kaposi’s sarcoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Data from South African ART and pediatric oncology programs revealed an overall cancer incidence of 82 per 100,000 person-years, with Kaposi’s sarcoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma being the most common. Although the incidence of AIDS-defining cancers has declined in the ART era, the risk of non-AIDS-defining cancers remains unchanged, underscoring the need for ongoing monitoring of children growing up with HIV. Multimorbidity is increasingly observed among young adults living with HIV on ART, particularly those aged 18–45 years. Adolescents with perinatally acquired HIV may be at higher risk of multimorbidity as they age, especially in resource-limited settings where primary prevention of noncommunicable diseases and management of inflammatory coinfections are inadequate. Existing service delivery platforms, such as early childhood development programs, under-five clinics, school-based services, and adolescent-friendly clinics, can be leveraged to screen for and manage noncommunicable diseases and comorbidities in children and adolescents living with HIV. Comprehensive HIV care for children and adolescents should include early ART initiation, growth and neurocognitive monitoring, screening for organ-specific diseases, mental health assessments, nutritional optimization, vaccination catch-up, and referrals to specialized care when needed. School-based programs and community-based psychosocial support services can further enhance care delivery. Research priorities include understanding the epidemiology and pathogenesis of noncommunicable diseases in children and adolescents living with HIV, developing population-specific definitions of comorbidities, and identifying optimal screening and management strategies. Validated, age-appropriate, and culturally relevant screening tools for mental health and neurocognitive disorders are urgently needed. Further studies on preventive and therapeutic interventions, including antibiotics, antivirals, anti-inflammatory drugs, and vitamin D, as well as educational and mental health programs, are essential. Additionally, the interactions of antiretroviral drugs used for prevention and treatment in children require further investigation.
